case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, in assessing Fourth Amendment excessive-force reasonableness, courts may consider an officer’s pre-shooting conduct and surrounding circumstances leading up to the use of deadly force, or must confine the analysis to the moment the trigger was pulled.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. IV (Fourth Amendment) — objective reasonableness standard for seizures (including use of force).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues the Fifth Circuit improperly narrowed the Fourth Amendment analysis by focusing only on the immediate instant of the shooting (the ‘moment-of-threat’ approach) and excluding relevant pre-shooting conduct that created or escalated the danger. Under Graham’s objective-reasonableness framework and the Fourth Amendment’s totality-of-the-circumstances test, the factfinder should be able to consider the full sequence of events that bear on whether the officer’s force was reasonable—including tactical decisions, escalation, and opportunities for de-escalation—rather than treating the shooting as a freestanding event divorced from what foreseeably led to it.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent contends the relevant Fourth Amendment inquiry is the objective reasonableness of the officer’s split-second decision at the time force was used, and that earlier acts are at most background and cannot transform a reasonable defensive use of deadly force into a constitutional violation. Respondent emphasizes Graham’s focus on what a reasonable officer would do in a rapidly evolving encounter, warning that expanding the scope to earlier conduct risks hindsight bias and improperly imposes negligence-like liability for tactical choices rather than judging the necessity of force when the threat materialized.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s and Justice Alito’s central objection—that any look-back invites negligence-style review and revives Mendez’s rejected “provocation” theory—deserves real weight, but it overreads Mendez: that case bars bootstrapping a separate Fourth Amendment violation to create excessive-force liability, not consideration of immediately antecedent facts that bear on what an objectively reasonable officer perceived and what options were reasonably apparent when force was used. At the same time, Justice Kavanaugh is right that an unbounded “foreseeability/alternatives” framing can become a proxy for best-practices policing, so the holding must be narrow: antecedent conduct is relevant only as contemporaneous context tightly connected to the force decision, and it cannot supply liability merely because different tactics might have reduced risk. That approach remains faithful to Graham’s “totality of the circumstances” while preserving institutional administrability and avoiding a de facto negligence regime. On that minimalist ground, I stay with Petitioner and would craft the opinion to emphasize that the inquiry remains focused on the reasonableness of the seizure, not on generalized critiques of police tactics.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s proposed “closely connected context” rule has surface appeal because Graham speaks of the “totality of the circumstances,” but that phrase cannot be read to convert the Fourth Amendment seizure inquiry into a back-looking assessment of police tactics that merely made the encounter riskier. As Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh warn, the foreseeability/alternatives framing advanced by Justice Kagan effectively imports negligence concepts and recreates, in substance, the bootstrapping problem County of Los Angeles v. Mendez rejected—using antecedent conduct to render an otherwise objectively reasonable defensive shooting unconstitutional absent an independent Fourth Amendment violation. Under Garner and Graham, the constitutional question remains whether the seizure was unreasonable when executed—i.e., whether an objectively reasonable officer faced an immediate threat justifying deadly force—while earlier errors may be actionable only as separate constitutional violations (if any) or under state tort law. I therefore do not see an argument that undermines the original public meaning focus on the reasonableness of the seizure itself.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s “middle position” is the most serious pro-Petitioner argument because, as Roberts and Barrett note, Graham’s “totality of the circumstances” cannot be a literal freeze-frame and some immediately antecedent facts inevitably supply context for what the officer reasonably perceived at the moment force was used. But Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s foreseeability/alternatives framing still slides the inquiry from the reasonableness of the seizure’s execution into a negligence-like audit of tactics, inviting liability whenever a court later identifies a different approach that might have reduced risk—precisely the hindsight Graham cautioned against. Mendez, as Justice Thomas emphasizes, bars using earlier police missteps to convert an otherwise objectively reasonable defensive shooting into an excessive-force violation absent an independent constitutional wrong; relabeling the same move as “closely connected context” or “foreseeable escalation” does not solve the bootstrapping problem in practice. I would allow antecedent facts only to illuminate the officer’s contemporaneous perceptions and the immediacy of the threat under Garner, while leaving antecedent tactical errors (if actionable) to separate constitutional claims or state tort remedies.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito’s strongest point—that looking to antecedent tactics risks converting Graham into negligence review and reviving Mendez’s rejected bootstrapping—does not justify a categorical moment-of-threat rule that Graham itself does not contain. As Chief Justice Roberts argues, the workable line is not “ignore what happened before,” but “consider only closely connected, encounter-defining facts insofar as they bear on what risks, alternatives, and perceptions were reasonably apparent when force was used,” which keeps the inquiry objective and contemporaneous rather than hindsight-laden. Mendez forecloses using a separate Fourth Amendment violation to manufacture excessive-force liability; it does not require courts to blind themselves to officers’ own immediately antecedent choices when assessing Garner’s necessity and proportionality within a single integrated reasonableness inquiry. Justice Kavanaugh’s concern about boundless foreseeability is real, but under a pragmatic, access-to-justice lens it is answered by requiring a tight nexus and excluding mere “better tactics” critiques—otherwise the Fourth Amendment would perversely insulate avoidable escalation that predictably increases lethal encounters for vulnerable communities.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and Justice Thomas’s core objection—that any look-back invites negligence-style second-guessing and revives Mendez under another label—has bite, but it overreads both Graham and Mendez. Graham’s textual command to assess the “totality of the circumstances” is not compatible with a categorical moment-of-threat cutoff, and Chief Justice Roberts’s framing answers the institutional worry by allowing antecedent facts only insofar as they illuminate what risks, alternatives, and perceptions were reasonably apparent at the time force was used, not to impose a free-standing duty of “better tactics.” Mendez forecloses bootstrapping from a separate Fourth Amendment violation (the provocation rule); it does not require courts to disregard tightly connected, encounter-defining facts within the single reasonableness inquiry—especially given Garner’s necessity/proportionality logic, which becomes incoherent if we must ignore objectively foreseeable, immediate precursors to the claimed “necessity.” Justice Kavanaugh’s concern about boundless “foreseeability” is real, but it is cabined by a relevance-and-close-connection requirement that keeps the inquiry objective and contemporaneous rather than a generalized negligence review.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito press the strongest point: the Fourth Amendment’s reasonableness inquiry must not become a negligence-style audit of police tactics, and Mendez rightly rejects turning earlier missteps into excessive-force liability by bootstrapping. But Chief Justice Roberts’s limiting principle answers that concern on the Fourth Amendment’s own terms—Graham’s “totality of the circumstances” does not admit a categorical “moment-of-threat” evidentiary cutoff, and antecedent facts may be considered only insofar as they illuminate what risks, alternatives, and perceptions were objectively apparent when the force was used. Properly applied, this is not a free-floating foreseeability test (as Justice Kavanaugh worries) but an ordinary relevance constraint within the single seizure’s reasonableness analysis, while leaving separate antecedent constitutional violations (if any) to be litigated as separate claims consistent with Mendez. The Respondent’s proposed snapshot rule is attractive as administrable, but it is not grounded in Graham’s text and would require courts to ignore encounter-defining facts that bear directly on necessity and proportionality under Garner.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s middle ground is the most serious pro-Petitioner point: Graham’s “totality of the circumstances” is not a literal freeze-frame, and some immediately antecedent facts can illuminate what the officer reasonably perceived when the force was used. But Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s foreseeability/alternatives framing still risks converting Graham and Garner into a de facto negligence review of tactics, effectively reviving the bootstrapping concern that Mendez rejected—by making an otherwise reasonable defensive shooting unconstitutional because earlier choices “foreseeably” increased danger. Under my institutionalist approach, the Fourth Amendment inquiry must stay tethered to whether the seizure’s execution was objectively reasonable at the time, with antecedent police mistakes addressed through separate constitutional claims (if independently unlawful) or tort law, not by diluting the reasonableness standard into best-practices litigation. Because Roberts’s proposal lacks a clear administrable line separating “context” from “tactics-based liability,” I would affirm for Respondent.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito rightly press that admitting antecedent tactics cannot become a backdoor negligence regime or revive Mendez’s rejected provocation theory, and their concern sharpens the need for a limiting principle. But Chief Justice Roberts’s formulation better fits Graham’s textual command to assess the “totality of the circumstances”: it does not impose a categorical moment-of-threat cutoff, yet it cabins pre-shooting facts to those closely connected to the seizure and relevant to what risks and alternatives were reasonably apparent when force was used. Properly understood, Mendez bars bootstrapping an independent constitutional violation to manufacture excessive-force liability; it does not require courts to ignore encounter-defining context within the single objective-reasonableness inquiry. That relevance-and-connection tether answers Justice Kavanaugh’s workability concern by preventing “foreseeability” from becoming a free-floating duty of care while preserving Garner’s necessity/proportionality analysis.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito’s strongest point—pre-shooting review risks converting Graham into negligence and reviving Mendez-style bootstrapping—does not warrant a categorical “moment-of-threat” cutoff that Graham’s “totality of the circumstances” language does not support. As Chief Justice Roberts frames it, Mendez bars using a separate Fourth Amendment violation to manufacture excessive-force liability, but it does not require courts to ignore encounter-defining, immediately antecedent facts that objectively shape what risks, alternatives, and perceptions were reasonably apparent when force was used—facts that are essential to applying Garner’s necessity inquiry coherently. Justice Kavanaugh is right that foreseeability can become limitless, yet Justice Kagan’s relevance-and-close-connection limit keeps the inquiry objective and tethered to the force decision without constitutionalizing “best practices.” Under a progressive pragmatic approach focused on procedural fairness and real-world incentives, excluding tightly connected antecedent conduct would skew reasonableness analysis toward avoidable escalation and reduce accountability in a way Graham does not command.

John Roberts.reasoning: Graham v. Connor requires an objective-reasonableness inquiry under the Fourth Amendment that turns on the totality of the circumstances, which ordinarily includes the sequence of events leading up to the seizure, not a rigid "moment-of-threat" snapshot. County of Los Angeles v. Mendez rejected the Ninth Circuit’s provocation rule—using a distinct Fourth Amendment violation to manufacture an excessive-force claim—but it did not foreclose considering pre-shooting conduct as part of Graham’s holistic reasonableness analysis. A narrow holding that courts may consider an officer’s pre-shooting conduct insofar as it bears on the reasonableness of the force used (while avoiding negligence-like hindsight review) best fits precedent and preserves institutional legitimacy by aligning doctrine with Graham’s established framework. Tennessee v. Garner likewise supports evaluating deadly force in light of the surrounding circumstances bearing on necessity and proportionality, not an isolated instant.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Fourth Amendment prohibits “unreasonable” seizures, and the relevant question is whether the seizure as executed—here, the use of deadly force—was objectively reasonable at the time it occurred. Graham v. Connor instructs courts to judge reasonableness from the perspective of a reasonable officer on the scene, accounting for the fact that officers must often make split-second judgments in tense and rapidly evolving circumstances; that framework does not authorize converting earlier tactical decisions into Fourth Amendment liability when the final use of force was justified by an immediate threat. Tennessee v. Garner likewise ties deadly force to the suspect’s posing an immediate danger at the time of the seizure, reinforcing that the constitutional inquiry turns on whether deadly force was necessary when applied, not on antecedent conduct that sounds in negligence. Expanding the inquiry to pre-shooting conduct risks untethering the Fourth Amendment from its text and original understanding as a limit on unreasonable seizures, and instead importing a freestanding duty of care better left to state tort law.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under the Fourth Amendment, the reasonableness of force is judged by an objective standard focused on the circumstances confronting the officer at the time force is used, particularly in “tense, uncertain, and rapidly evolving” situations. Graham v. Connor requires assessment of the immediate threat and split-second judgments, and expanding the inquiry to broadly re-litigate pre-shooting tactics risks importing negligence concepts and hindsight bias into a constitutional standard. County of Los Angeles v. Mendez rejects using prior police missteps to “manufacture” an excessive-force violation where the defensive use of force was otherwise reasonable, permitting liability for antecedent Fourth Amendment violations only on their own terms rather than as a bootstrap for the shooting. Courts may consider surrounding context to understand the moment of force, but they should not treat earlier tactical decisions, absent an independent constitutional violation, as determinative of Fourth Amendment excessive-force liability.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Fourth Amendment’s objective-reasonableness inquiry under Graham v. Connor requires assessing the “totality of the circumstances,” and that does not begin only at the instant the trigger is pulled; it includes the facts and choices that foreseeably shaped the danger and the necessity for deadly force. Tennessee v. Garner reinforces that deadly force must be necessary and proportional in context, and context necessarily includes whether officers had feasible opportunities to slow down, de-escalate, or avoid creating the very confrontation used to justify killing. County of Los Angeles v. Mendez properly rejects using a separate Fourth Amendment violation to “manufacture” an excessive-force claim, but it does not mandate a blinkered moment-of-threat approach; rather, it leaves room to consider pre-shooting conduct as part of the Graham totality analysis without converting negligence into strict liability. Limiting courts to the split-second of firing undermines accountability and disproportionately harms vulnerable people by insulating plainly avoidable escalations from meaningful Fourth Amendment review.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Graham v. Connor directs courts to assess Fourth Amendment force claims under an objective “totality of the circumstances” inquiry, which textually and practically encompasses the full sequence of events bearing on whether the seizure was reasonable—not an artificially narrowed “moment-of-threat” snapshot. Tennessee v. Garner likewise frames deadly-force reasonableness around necessity and proportionality in light of the surrounding facts, which can include foreseeable danger created or escalated by officers’ own tactical choices. County of Los Angeles v. Mendez rejected using a separate Fourth Amendment violation to “manufacture” an excessive-force claim, but it did not foreclose considering pre-shooting conduct as part of Graham’s reasonableness analysis, and indeed left that question open. A workable rule is that earlier conduct may be considered insofar as it is causally and foreseeably connected to the need for force, while still judging the ultimate use of force by an objective standard that avoids hindsight bias.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Fourth Amendment’s text and this Court’s cases require an objective-reasonableness inquiry that accounts for the “totality of the circumstances,” not an artificially frozen snapshot limited to the instant the trigger is pulled. Graham v. Connor directs courts to evaluate reasonableness by considering all facts bearing on the seizure, and nothing in its standard authorizes a categorical “moment-of-threat” rule that excludes an officer’s immediately antecedent choices that foreseeably created or escalated the confrontation. County of Los Angeles v. Mendez properly rejects using an earlier, separate Fourth Amendment violation to "manufacture" an excessive-force claim (the provocation rule), but it does not compel ignoring relevant pre-shooting circumstances within the same encounter when applying Graham’s objective test. Confined to Fourth Amendment reasonableness (and not negligence), factfinders may weigh pre-shooting conduct as part of the circumstances without collapsing the inquiry into hindsight liability.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under the Fourth Amendment’s objective-reasonableness standard, Graham v. Connor instructs courts to evaluate the use of force from the perspective of a reasonable officer facing a rapidly evolving situation, with particular attention to the split-second judgment at the time force is applied. County of Los Angeles v. Mendez reinforces that earlier officer conduct cannot be used to "manufacture" an excessive-force violation by converting a later, otherwise reasonable shooting into an unreasonable seizure, even if earlier actions were flawed. While surrounding circumstances inform the context, the constitutional question remains whether the officer’s decision to use deadly force was reasonable at the moment it was used, and prior tactical missteps are better addressed, if at all, through separate claims for independent Fourth Amendment violations and ordinary causation principles. Limiting the inquiry this way promotes workability and reduces hindsight bias consistent with judicial restraint and precedent.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Fourth Amendment’s reasonableness inquiry is textually and doctrinally a “totality of the circumstances” test, and nothing in the Amendment’s original public meaning or in Graham v. Connor authorizes courts to artificially slice the “circumstances” down to the instant the trigger is pulled. Graham directs an objective assessment of what a reasonable officer would do in light of the facts confronting him, which can include immediately antecedent decisions that foreseeably created or escalated the confrontation, so long as the analysis remains objective and not a backdoor negligence standard. County of Los Angeles v. Mendez properly rejects using a separate constitutional violation to “manufacture” an excessive-force claim (the provocation rule), but it does not require a moment-of-threat rule and leaves room to consider pre-shooting context as part of the single Graham reasonableness inquiry. Tennessee v. Garner likewise evaluates deadly force against the surrounding circumstances bearing on necessity, reinforcing that the shooting is not a freestanding event divorced from its precipitating context.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Fourth Amendment’s objective-reasonableness inquiry under Graham v. Connor requires assessing the totality of the circumstances, which logically includes the officers’ reasonably foreseeable pre-shooting conduct that shaped the encounter and the need for force, not just the instant the trigger was pulled. Tennessee v. Garner likewise ties deadly-force permissibility to necessity under the circumstances, and courts cannot evaluate “necessity” while artificially excising the immediately antecedent tactical choices and opportunities for de-escalation that bear on whether force was avoidable. County of Los Angeles v. Mendez rejected the Ninth Circuit’s “provocation rule” (using a separate Fourth Amendment violation to bootstrap an excessive-force claim), but it did not foreclose considering pre-shooting conduct as part of the Graham reasonableness analysis from the outset. Confining review to a “moment-of-threat” snapshot risks undermining procedural fairness by insulating escalation tactics from constitutional scrutiny and produces impractical incentives inconsistent with the Fourth Amendment’s real-world constraints on state violence.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, in assessing a Fourth Amendment excessive-force claim, courts may consider officers’ conduct and circumstances leading up to the moment force was used (the “totality of the circumstances”), or must evaluate reasonableness using a narrow snapshot limited to the instant the force was applied.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. IV (Fourth Amendment) — objective reasonableness standard for seizures/excessive force under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (and parallel standards for federal officers).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues the Fifth Circuit’s approach improperly narrows the Graham v. Connor “totality of the circumstances” inquiry by focusing almost exclusively on the split-second when the shot was fired, disregarding earlier police actions that foreseeably created, escalated, or shaped the need to use deadly force. Petitioner contends that Fourth Amendment reasonableness must account for the full chain of events (including tactical choices, opportunity for de-escalation, and avoidable escalation) because those facts bear directly on whether the eventual use of deadly force was objectively reasonable.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent argues the Fourth Amendment reasonableness inquiry properly centers on what the officer reasonably perceived at the moment deadly force was used, especially in fast-evolving encounters, and that earlier events (including alleged tactical mistakes) should not transform an otherwise reasonable split-second decision into a constitutional violation. Respondent emphasizes officer safety and the need to judge force from the perspective of a reasonable officer on the scene, warning that broader hindsight review would second-guess policing decisions and expand liability beyond established law.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh make the strongest opposing point that Mendez warns against “manufacturing” excessive-force liability out of earlier missteps, and I agree that Graham cannot be converted into a negligence-style tactics audit by hindsight. But Justice Kagan is right that Mendez rejected a distinct provocation rule; it did not authorize the Fifth Circuit’s categorical “snapshot” evidentiary cutoff that strips Graham’s “totality of the circumstances” of content and invites arbitrary line-drawing about what counts as the relevant moment. Justice Thomas’s text-and-seizure framing properly cabins the inquiry to the reasonableness of the seizure, yet the objective reasonableness of that seizure still depends on context that bears on contemporaneous perception and the realistic options available when force was used. The narrow, institutionally modest course is to reject only the categorical snapshot rule and remand for a fact-bound Graham/Garner application that permits antecedent facts solely to the extent they illuminate the split-second decision, without any provocation-style bootstrapping.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s reliance on Graham’s “totality of the circumstances” does not justify converting the Fourth Amendment’s regulation of a “seizure” into a broader judicial review of antecedent tactics: the relevant “circumstances” are those bearing on the objective reasonableness of the force at the time it is applied. As Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, Mendez’s warning against “manufactur[ing]” excessive-force liability confirms that courts may not fold earlier, arguably negligent escalation into the seizure’s reasonableness as a causation-style theory; prior illegality should be pursued, if at all, as a distinct Fourth Amendment claim. I agree with the Chief Justice that we need not defend a rigid “single-instant” evidentiary cutoff, but any consideration of earlier events must be limited to facts that illuminate what the officer reasonably perceived “on the scene” in that split-second—not to second-guess alternative tactics in hindsight. Because Petitioners’ approach risks untethering the analysis from the seizure itself and diluting Graham/Garner into a negligence regime, I remain with the Respondent.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right that Graham’s “totality of the circumstances” cannot support a categorical evidentiary cutoff, and I do not defend a wooden “single-instant” rule. But their “options reasonably available/foreseeably escalatory choices” framing risks the very bootstrapping Mendez cautioned against—converting antecedent tactical judgments into a causation-like theory that renders an otherwise reasonable split-second seizure unconstitutional. Under Garner and Graham, the constitutional question remains whether, at the time force was used, the officer had an objectively reasonable basis to perceive an immediate significant threat; antecedent facts are relevant only insofar as they inform that contemporaneous perception, not as an after-the-fact audit of alternative tactics. Justice Sotomayor’s concern about avoidable escalation is better addressed through separate Fourth Amendment claims for earlier illegality (if any) or through policy, rather than diluting the administrable moment-of-seizure inquiry.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh raise the hardest point—Mendez’s warning against “manufacturing” excessive-force liability from antecedent missteps—but that warning targets a provocation doctrine that made an earlier violation dispositive, not Graham’s ordinary totality inquiry when antecedent facts objectively shape the immediacy of the threat and the feasible alternatives at the moment force is used. Justice Thomas is right to insist the Fourth Amendment regulates the reasonableness of the seizure, yet “reasonableness” has never been acontextual: excluding encounter-shaping facts risks converting Graham into an artificial one-instant snapshot that distorts necessity and proportionality under Garner. The administrable middle ground the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan describe—rejecting a categorical cutoff while limiting antecedent conduct to its bearing on contemporaneous perception and options—answers hindsight concerns without insulating foreseeable escalation that disproportionately endangers vulnerable people. I therefore remain with Petitioner to vacate the Fifth Circuit’s categorical snapshot rule and remand for a fact-bound Graham analysis.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh are right to press Mendez’s warning against “manufacturing” excessive-force liability out of earlier mistakes, but that concern is addressed by a limiting principle, not by the Fifth Circuit’s categorical snapshot rule. As the Chief Justice notes, Graham’s "totality of the circumstances" language is not surplusage; it requires admitting antecedent facts when they bear on the objective officer-on-the-scene assessment of immediacy, necessity, and proportionality at the moment force is used, while still forbidding hindsight “tactics audits” untethered to that moment. Justice Thomas’s seizure-focused framing properly rejects converting negligence into a Fourth Amendment violation, yet excluding encounter-shaping context that a reasonable officer would have experienced makes the Graham inquiry artificially incoherent and less administrable, not more. The workable middle ground is to reject a categorical cutoff and remand with instruction that pre-seizure conduct is relevant only insofar as it illuminates the contemporaneous reasonableness of the seizure, consistent with Mendez’s rejection of provocation-style bootstrapping.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right to resist a categorical “snapshot” evidentiary cutoff because Graham’s “totality of the circumstances” language is real, and some antecedent facts will necessarily inform what an officer perceived in the split-second decision. But Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett correctly emphasize that the Fourth Amendment’s object is the reasonableness of the seizure itself, and Graham’s anti-hindsight instruction—reinforced by Mendez’s warning against “manufactur[ing]” excessive-force liability from earlier missteps—precludes converting pre-seizure tactics into a negligence-like escalation review untethered to what the officer reasonably perceived and faced when force was applied. Petitioners’ broader framing about “foreseeable escalation” and “available alternatives” risks collapsing distinct Fourth Amendment theories into one open-ended reasonableness inquiry, whereas earlier unconstitutional searches or seizures can (and should) be challenged directly without bootstrapping them into the later use-of-force claim. I would therefore uphold a rule that permits antecedent evidence only insofar as it bears on contemporaneous threat perception and constraints at the moment of force, while rejecting any approach that treats earlier tactical choices as an independent basis to deem an otherwise reasonable seizure unreasonable.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right that Graham’s “totality of the circumstances” language resists a wooden evidentiary cutoff, and I agree we should not constitutionalize a literal one-instant “snapshot” that excludes context necessary to understand what the officer perceived. But their proposed permission to weigh antecedent “options” and “foreseeably escalatory choices” risks the very bootstrapping Mendez warned against—turning earlier tactical missteps into a causation-based path to Fourth Amendment liability for a seizure that was objectively reasonable when applied. As Justice Thomas and Justice Alito emphasize, Graham and Garner center the constitutional inquiry on the officer’s split-second threat assessment at the moment of force; antecedent facts are admissible only insofar as they illuminate that contemporaneous perception, not as a freestanding escalation audit. Under an institutionalist, precedent-bound approach, I would affirm the need to keep excessive-force doctrine administrable and tethered to the seizure itself while leaving separate claims to address any earlier illegality.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right that Graham’s “totality of the circumstances” language resists a wooden, one-instant evidentiary cutoff, and I agree the Fifth Circuit should not be read to impose an absolute bar on antecedent facts. But that concession does not answer the core Fourth Amendment question, which—under Graham’s repeated admonitions to avoid “20/20 hindsight” and to judge from the perspective of a reasonable officer “on the scene,” and under Garner’s focus on probable cause to perceive a significant threat when deadly force is used—cabins relevance to circumstances bearing on the officer’s contemporaneous threat assessment and feasible options at that moment. Justice Sotomayor’s view that foreseeable escalation should enter the reasonableness balance risks, in my view, recreating the negligence-like “tactics audit” that Mendez cautioned against by “manufactur[ing]” excessive-force liability from earlier missteps rather than evaluating the seizure itself. So while I would clarify that some pre-seizure context may be admissible for the narrow purpose Justice Thomas describes, I do not think Petitioners have shown the Fifth Circuit’s moment-of-seizure focus is legally erroneous as a constitutional standard.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh offer the strongest objection: Mendez’s anti-“manufacture” logic and Graham’s anti-hindsight admonition caution against turning earlier tactics into negligence-by-another-name. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, rejecting a categorical Fifth Circuit “snapshot” cutoff does not adopt a provocation rule; it simply restores Graham’s required “totality of the circumstances” inquiry while cabining antecedent facts to those that objectively bear on the officer’s contemporaneous threat assessment, necessity, and proportionality at the moment force is used. Justice Thomas’s seizure-focused textual framing usefully limits the claim to the reasonableness of the seizure itself, yet “reasonableness” cannot be evaluated fairly if courts are forbidden to consider encounter-shaping facts that are part of what a reasonable officer would confront and what realistic alternatives existed in that moment. The administrable middle ground is therefore to reverse the categorical cutoff and clarify that prior conduct is relevant only insofar as it illuminates the Graham/Garner balance at the time of the seizure, not as an independent basis for liability.

John Roberts.reasoning: Graham v. Connor directs courts to assess objective reasonableness under the Fourth Amendment by “careful attention to the facts and circumstances of each particular case,” i.e., the totality of the circumstances, rather than an artificially narrow snapshot of the instant force is applied. Tennessee v. Garner likewise frames the inquiry as a balancing that depends not only on when a seizure occurs but also how it is carried out, which necessarily permits consideration of relevant events leading up to the use of force. Because this Court has not held that pre-seizure conduct is categorically excluded, the Fifth Circuit’s near-exclusive focus on the split-second of firing is difficult to reconcile with our precedent and risks creating an unduly rigid rule. A narrow disposition would hold only that earlier conduct may be considered insofar as it bears on the objective reasonableness of the force used, leaving case-specific application to lower courts under § 1983.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Fourth Amendment’s text forbids only “unreasonable” seizures, and the relevant “seizure” in an excessive-force case is the application of force itself; thus the reasonableness inquiry must focus on the objective circumstances confronting the officer at the moment force is used, not on antecedent tactical choices. Graham v. Connor requires an objective, on-the-scene assessment that avoids “20/20 vision of hindsight,” and it frames the analysis around the severity of the crime, immediacy of the threat, and resistance/flight as they bear on the officer’s split-second decision. Tennessee v. Garner likewise ties deadly-force reasonableness to whether the officer has probable cause to believe the suspect poses a significant threat at the time of the seizure. Expanding Fourth Amendment liability to encompass pre-seizure conduct risks converting negligence in policing into constitutional tort and exceeds the Amendment’s original public meaning and limited scope.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Graham v. Connor requires an objective-reasonableness inquiry judged “from the perspective of a reasonable officer on the scene,” and it repeatedly warns against 20/20 hindsight in rapidly evolving encounters; that text and framing point the analysis toward the circumstances as they reasonably appeared at the moment force was used. Tennessee v. Garner likewise focuses deadly-force reasonableness on the immediate threat posed at the time of the seizure, not on antecedent tactical decisions that may have contributed to the confrontation. County of Los Angeles v. Mendez rejected expanding Graham through doctrines that effectively convert prior police missteps into Fourth Amendment excessive-force liability, underscoring the practical danger of second-guessing split-second judgments and deterring proactive law enforcement. While earlier facts may provide context, the Constitution does not make an otherwise reasonable on-the-spot decision unreasonable merely because different tactics might have avoided the need for force.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Fourth Amendment’s objective reasonableness inquiry under Graham v. Connor requires courts to evaluate the “totality of the circumstances,” not a contrived snapshot that begins only at the instant force is applied. Tennessee v. Garner likewise frames reasonableness as a balance that turns on not only when a seizure occurs but how it is carried out, which necessarily can include officers’ preceding choices that foreseeably escalated the encounter and shaped the perceived need for deadly force. Nothing in this Court’s precedents categorically excludes pre-seizure conduct from the reasonableness analysis, and a narrow moment-of-force rule would distort Graham’s fact-bound balancing and diminish accountability where avoidable escalation harms vulnerable individuals. Accordingly, courts may consider the chain of events leading up to the use of force as part of the Fourth Amendment analysis under 42 U.S.C. § 1983.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Graham v. Connor requires assessing objective reasonableness under the Fourth Amendment based on the “totality of the circumstances,” which naturally includes officers’ actions and situational developments that bear on whether the need for force was reasonably perceived and whether that need was avoidably created. County of Los Angeles v. Mendez properly rejects using a separate Fourth Amendment violation to “manufacture” an excessive-force claim (the provocation rule), but it does not foreclose considering pre-force conduct as part of the same Graham reasonableness inquiry when it helps explain the threat assessment and available alternatives. A rigid snapshot rule risks incoherent doctrine by treating the decisive moment as context-free, even though the reasonableness of that moment often depends on how the encounter was initiated and escalated. Limiting evidence to the instant of force also undermines workability by inviting arbitrary line-drawing about what counts as the “moment” of seizure rather than applying a consistent totality analysis.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Fourth Amendment asks whether the particular seizure was “reasonable,” and Graham v. Connor directs an objective assessment from the perspective of a reasonable officer on the scene, accounting for the need to make split-second judgments rather than retrospective second-guessing. A rule that expands the excessive-force inquiry to encompass earlier tactical errors risks collapsing distinct Fourth Amendment questions into one and, as County of Los Angeles v. Mendez explains, “manufactur[ing] an excessive force claim where one would not otherwise exist” by leveraging antecedent conduct. Petitioners remain free to pursue separate Fourth Amendment claims for earlier unconstitutional searches or seizures, but the force inquiry itself properly centers on the facts bearing on the officer’s perception and the immediate threat at the moment force was used, consistent with Graham and Tennessee v. Garner. This approach also respects separation-of-powers limits by avoiding judge-made liability standards untethered to the Amendment’s text or this Court’s settled framework.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Graham v. Connor, the Fourth Amendment excessive-force inquiry turns on “objective reasonableness” from the perspective of a reasonable officer on the scene, accounting for the fact that officers often must make split-second judgments in tense and rapidly evolving situations; that framework supports focusing primarily on the circumstances as the force was applied. County of Los Angeles v. Mendez reinforces that courts may not use earlier alleged police missteps (or even other constitutional violations) to “manufacture” an excessive-force violation where the seizure itself was otherwise reasonable, counseling against an open-ended hindsight review of pre-seizure tactics. Tennessee v. Garner supplies the substantive limit on deadly force (immediate threat/serious harm), which likewise is evaluated at the point the officer confronts that threat. As an institutional matter, a moment-of-threat focus is more workable and consistent with precedent, leaving claims about earlier misconduct to be litigated as separate Fourth Amendment violations (e.g., unlawful entry) rather than folded into the force analysis.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Fourth Amendment asks whether the “seizure” was objectively reasonable, and Graham v. Connor directs courts to judge that reasonableness from the perspective of a reasonable officer on the scene, particularly in tense, rapidly evolving encounters. While Graham speaks of the “totality of the circumstances,” County of Los Angeles v. Mendez rejected using earlier constitutional violations or “bad tactics” to manufacture an excessive-force claim where the force at the moment of seizure was otherwise reasonable, and it expressly declined to adopt a broader causation-style inquiry. Textually, the Amendment targets “unreasonable searches and seizures,” and the seizure at issue is the use of force itself; earlier conduct may be relevant only insofar as it informs what the officer reasonably perceived when force was applied, not as a free-standing basis to deem a reasonable split-second use of force unconstitutional. Consistent with precedent and methodological consistency, the reasonableness analysis should remain centered on the moment force was used, with limited contextual consideration tied to that moment rather than a wide-ranging retrospective review.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Graham v. Connor requires an objective-reasonableness inquiry that turns on the “totality of the circumstances,” not a doctrinally imposed snapshot that artificially excludes earlier police conduct that foreseeably created, escalated, or constrained the encounter. Consistent with Tennessee v. Garner’s emphasis on necessity and proportionality in the use of deadly force, courts may consider pre-force tactical choices and opportunities for de-escalation insofar as they bear on whether the ultimate seizure was reasonable under the Fourth Amendment. County of Los Angeles v. Mendez properly rejects using a separate Fourth Amendment violation to “manufacture” an excessive-force claim, but it does not bar considering antecedent facts as part of the same Graham reasonableness analysis of the forceful seizure itself. A rule that looks only to the instant the trigger is pulled risks undermining procedural fairness and invites avoidable harms by insulating unreasonable escalation from constitutional scrutiny under 42 U.S.C. § 1983.
